lesson.title: When Positive Finds Negative Next Door
lesson.summary: Dipole-dipole forces are attractions between the permanent partial charges of neighboring polar molecules, adding an extra layer of intermolecular attraction on top of the London dispersion forces already present in every substance.
lesson.body:
Dipole-dipole forces are the intermolecular attractions that occur specifically between polar molecules, the ones that, as established when molecular polarity and dipole moment were introduced, carry a permanent separation of partial positive and partial negative charge. Unlike the temporary, fluctuating dipoles responsible for London dispersion forces, a polar molecule's dipole is fixed by its structure, always present rather than flickering in and out of existence. When two polar molecules come near each other, they tend to orient so that the partial positive end of one molecule sits near the partial negative end of its neighbor, and this consistent, favorable alignment produces a steady attractive force between them.

Hydrogen chloride, HCl, offers a clean example. Its dipole moment, arising from the significant electronegativity difference between hydrogen and chlorine, gives each molecule a permanent partial positive charge on hydrogen and partial negative charge on chlorine. In liquid or solid HCl, molecules arrange themselves so that the positive hydrogen end of one molecule points toward the negative chlorine end of a neighbor, and it takes real energy to pull molecules out of that favorable arrangement, which is exactly why HCl has a measurably higher boiling point than nonpolar molecules of comparable mass and electron count. Comparing HCl to F2 makes this concrete: the two have similar molar mass and similar total electron count, so their London dispersion forces are roughly comparable, yet HCl boils at a noticeably higher temperature because it has dipole-dipole forces acting in addition to dispersion forces, while F2, being nonpolar, has only dispersion forces to overcome.

It is important to be precise about how dipole-dipole forces combine with dispersion forces rather than replacing them. As emphasized when intermolecular forces were first introduced, London dispersion forces act between essentially all molecules regardless of polarity, so a polar molecule experiences dispersion forces plus dipole-dipole forces layered on top, never dipole-dipole forces alone. This is why the strength ranking of dispersion weaker than dipole-dipole is a statement about the added increment of attraction that polarity contributes, holding molecular size roughly constant, rather than a claim that polar molecules automatically have stronger overall attraction than every nonpolar molecule; a sufficiently large nonpolar molecule can still have stronger total intermolecular attraction than a small polar one, precisely because its dispersion forces, boosted by high polarizability, can outweigh a modest dipole-dipole contribution elsewhere.

Dipole-dipole forces are, on a molecule for molecule basis at similar size, generally stronger than dispersion forces alone but weaker than hydrogen bonding, the especially strong special case of dipole-dipole attraction covered next. This places dipole-dipole forces as the middle tier of the intermolecular strength ranking developed across this chapter, and recognizing them requires exactly the same skill built in the polar and nonpolar molecule sections: check the molecule's geometry and bond dipoles for a net dipole moment, and if one exists, dipole-dipole forces are present alongside the dispersion forces that are already there in every case.
